## Approach

I ranked candidate conditions by how well the 100 measured edits separate when the condition holds versus when it doesn't. I then kept the ones that also make sense structurally.

## Main pattern

The largest and most reliable interactions come from **output connectivity**. If an edit creates or removes the only path into node 3, the effect is 30–78 points, in the same direction on all three datasets. Examples:

- **Adding a path into a disconnected output:** experiments 6, 85 and 91 gained between +21.90 and +77.80 points.
- **Deleting the last path into the output:** experiments 21 and 29 lost between −31.46 and −77.90 points.

When parallel edges into node 3 already exist, the same edits change accuracy by only a few points.

## Second pattern

The other hypotheses come from **what operation an edit replaces**:

- **Replacing a 3×3 convolution with a cheaper op** (skip or average pool) tends to lose accuracy (experiments 43, 47, 49, 54, 58, 87, 90).
- **Replacing a weak op** (average pool or `none`) tends to gain.
- **Adding a 3×3 convolution on edge 5** helps more when node 2's input is not already a convolution (experiments 13 vs 14, 15 vs 16, 17 vs 18).

## Caveats

- Hypotheses 1–6 rest on many experiments with large, same-signed gaps, so I'm fairly confident in them.
- Hypotheses 7, 8 and 10 rest on gaps of only a few points, often from 3–4 contrasts, so they are the most likely to fail the "consistent across all three datasets" test.
- The datasets are noisy at the ±2–4 point level. ImageNet16-120 in particular often disagrees with the other two on small effects.
